lines: A toy log, hundreds of records deep, with nothing sorted for lookup.
Reading one near the end by starting from the very beginning touches almost every record on the way there.
Reading that exact same record a second way touches only a handful. Nothing about the data changed between the two. What changed is how it was found.
Worth being precise about what a partition actually is, before going further.
It isn't some abstract queue sitting in memory somewhere. It's a folder of ordinary files, sitting on a real disk.
One of those files is still being written to. Every other one is finished, and nothing in it will ever change again.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
The file currently being written to has just reached its size limit.
The next record still has to land somewhere. Does the write simply wait? Does something old get thrown away to make room? Or does something else happen entirely?
answer: A new file opens, and the write lands there instead.
A size limit on one file isn't a ceiling on the whole partition. It's just the point where that file stops growing and a fresh one starts.
Throwing away an old file is a completely different decision, made on its own schedule, never triggered just because the newest file happened to fill up.

lines: Here's that happening for real, not just argued for.
Records keep landing, one after another, and the file currently open keeps growing with them.
The moment it crosses its real configured limit, a new file opens, and it happens again, more than once, over the course of one ordinary run.
Every one of those records landed somewhere in a log file. A second, much smaller file sits beside it, and it's worth asking what that one actually tracks.
It doesn't name a byte position for every single record — that would make it almost as large as the log itself.
It only checks in every so often. A handful of checkpoints is enough to get a search close, and a short walk forward from there finds the exact record.
Worth asking directly, before trusting it any further.
That index only checks in occasionally, not on every record.
Does skipping most records like that risk a seek ever coming back with the wrong one?
answer: Never. The index only narrows a search down to roughly the right spot.
A short, exact scan from there always finds the one record actually asked for, every single time.

lines: One more piece of the picture is worth opening: what actually happens when bytes travel from that disk to whoever's reading them.
The ordinary way means copying the same bytes back and forth between the operating system and the program reading them, more than once, before a single byte ever reaches the network.

The real design skips most of that. The operating system already keeps a copy of recently read data in its own memory, and a single call hands that exact copy straight to the network, with nothing extra in between.
One more question worth asking directly: who actually remembers how far a reader has gotten through a partition?
Not the system holding the data. The reader keeps that number itself, entirely on its own side.

Which means a reader can step that number backward on purpose and read something it already read before, and nothing about the underlying files has to know, or care, that it happened — checked directly, byte for byte, before and after.
Every number shown so far came from one real run, happening just now, not a diagram drawn ahead of time.
The size at which a file actually rolled, and how many checkpoints a sparse file ended up holding against how many records actually exist.
How many records each kind of search actually had to look at to find the identical one, and a reader stepping backward, checked to change nothing at all.
A partition, then, is nothing more mysterious than files on a disk, one of them still growing.
A size limit that starts a fresh file rather than blocking anything.
A small index that checks in occasionally and still finds anything quickly.
A read path that hands over memory the system already had sitting ready, with almost nothing copied twice.
And a reader's own position, which belongs to the reader alone, and nobody else.
